Getting started: how accessible is GP care in Cornwall?

Source: vignettes/spax.Rmd
spax.Rmd

This guide measures how accessible general practice (GP) care is across mainland Cornwall and maps the answer. By the end you will understand the idea behind a floating catchment area (FCA) index, compute one from a population grid, a table of practices and travel times, and read its map. The data are the open Cornwall GP data that ship with spax, described in The Cornwall GP example data. The spax() interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

The guide uses spax with terra for grids, sf and dplyr for tables and ggplot2 for the practices map.

library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The question

Some residents live next to a practice with many GPs. Others live far from any practice, or near one that many people share. An accessibility index puts both into one number per place: the supply of a service (here GP full-time equivalents, FTE) relative to the demand that competes for it (here residents), with distant practices counting for less. Where in Cornwall is that number high, and where is it low?

The idea in two steps

An FCA index answers the question in two steps. A tiny example with three areas and two practices shows both. The weights say how much each practice counts for each area: 1 next door, less further away.

# Residents of three areas, and GP FTE at two practices
demand <- c(village = 1000, town = 4000, coast = 2000)
supply <- c(north = 3, south = 2)

# Weight of each practice (columns) for each area (rows)
weights <- rbind(
  village = c(north = 1.0, south = 0.1),
  town    = c(north = 0.5, south = 0.5),
  coast   = c(north = 0.1, south = 1.0)
)
weights
        north south
village   1.0   0.1
town      0.5   0.5
coast     0.1   1.0

The village is next to the north practice, the coast next to the south practice, and the town lies between the two.

Step 1. Each practice gathers the residents around it, each counted with its weight, and divides its GP FTE by that weighted count.

# For each practice: residents times weight, summed over the areas
gathered <- colSums(weights * demand)
gathered
north south 
 3200  4100 
# GP FTE per 1,000 weighted residents
ratio <- supply / gathered
round(1000 * ratio, 2)
north south 
 0.94  0.49

The north practice has 3 GP FTE for 3,200 weighted residents, about 0.94 per 1,000. The south practice has 2 for 4,100, about 0.49 per 1,000.

Step 2. Each area adds up the ratios of the practices around it, weighted again.

# For each area: practice ratios times weight, summed over the practices
index <- drop(weights %*% ratio)
round(1000 * index, 2)
village    town   coast 
   0.99    0.71    0.58 
# Residents times the index, summed over the areas
sum(index * demand)
[1] 5

The village leans on the better-supplied north practice and scores highest, at 0.99 GP FTE per 1,000 residents. The coast leans on the south practice and scores lowest, at 0.58. Residents times the index add up to the 5 GP FTE of the two practices: the index shares the supply out among residents and creates none.

The weighted residents around a practice are its catchment, which floats with the practice instead of following area borders. With weights of only 1 within a travel-time limit and 0 beyond it, these two steps are the original two-step FCA (2SFCA). Graded weights, as here, give the enhanced two-step FCA, or E2SFCA. In a real study the weights come from travel times through a decay curve, and spax computes them for every place and every practice. With the curve used below, a weight of 0.5 means about 12 minutes away and 0.1 about 21 minutes.

The Cornwall data

spax ships open data for GP care in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly: the 55 practices with their GP FTE, 337 small areas with their registered residents, who is registered at which practice, and travel times. A population grid of about 1 km cells and one layer of travel minutes per practice cover the same area. The Isles of Scilly have no road link to the mainland, so the guides use mainland Cornwall only, with its 54 practices. The Cornwall GP example data describes each object, its sources and its limits. The map shows the mainland practices, sized by their GP FTE, with a few towns named for reference.

# Mainland practices and small areas, with their geometry
practices <- filter(cornwall_gp, !scilly)
small_areas <- filter(cornwall_lsoa, !scilly)
outline <- st_union(small_areas)

# A few towns, by longitude and latitude, to find places on the maps
towns <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(
    town = c("Penzance", "Helston", "Redruth", "Truro", "Falmouth", "Bodmin", "Bude", "Launceston"),
    lon = c(-5.54, -5.27, -5.23, -5.05, -5.07, -4.72, -4.54, -4.36),
    lat = c(50.12, 50.10, 50.23, 50.26, 50.15, 50.47, 50.83, 50.64)
  ),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = small_areas,
    fill = "grey95",
    color = "grey70",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = practices,
    aes(size = gp_fte_extg),
    shape = 21,
    fill = "orange",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = outline, fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf_text(
    data = towns, aes(label = town), size = 3, vjust = -0.9,
    fun.geometry = sf::st_centroid
  ) +
  scale_size_area(name = "GP FTE") +
  labs(title = "GP practices in mainland Cornwall") +
  theme_void()

Practices are densest in the west, around Redruth, Truro and Falmouth. The largest has 13.4 GP FTE. Bodmin Moor, the upland north-east of Bodmin, has none.

Compute the index

An FCA index needs three inputs that line up: a population grid of residents per cell (demand), a table of practices with their GP FTE (supply), and a stack of travel-time grids with one layer of minutes per practice, named by practice code. These lines read them and keep the mainland cells that have a travel time to every practice. Every FCA guide starts from them.

gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

gp is the practices table without its map geometry. prep_data() takes the table and holds the three inputs together. id_col names the column of practice codes that matches the travel layers, and supply_cols the column of supply.

spec_e2sfca() says which index to compute and how. spax() then computes it on grid_data. The decay turns travel minutes into weights. Here it is a Gaussian curve whose travel scale σ, in minutes, sets how fast the weights fall. With σ = 10, a practice 10 minutes away counts about 61% as much as one next door, and one 20 minutes away about 14%. The scale is a choice for this guide. Where do residents register? estimates a travel scale from observed registrations. This line computes the index on the Cornwall data and prints a summary.

e2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))
e2sfca
<spax access> E2SFCA, 1 layer on 117 x 187 cells

Spatial Properties:
- Resolution: 0.00833333 x 0.00833333
- Dimensions: 117 x 187

Measures: 1
- gp_fte_extg

Facilities: 54

Parameters:
- Decay function: gaussian (sigma = 10)
- Demand normalization: identity

The print gives the grid: 117 rows by 187 columns of cells about 1 km across (the resolution is in degrees, 30 arc-seconds). It also gives the supply column it used (gp_fte_extg), the 54 practices and the settings: the Gaussian decay with σ = 10, and the default normalization identity, which uses the weights unchanged when practices gather residents. The accessibility member is the index on the grid, a raster in GP FTE per resident. We map it per 1,000 residents, with the practices as red crosses and the same towns named.

# Practice and town locations in the grid's coordinates (longitude and latitude)
practice_points <- vect(practices)
town_points <- vect(towns)
outline_lonlat <- vect(outline)

plot(
  1000 * e2sfca$accessibility,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  main = "E2SFCA: GP FTE per 1,000 residents (Gaussian, sigma = 10 min)"
)
lines(outline_lonlat, lwd = 0.6)
points(practice_points, pch = 3, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
text(town_points, labels = town_points$town, pos = 3, cex = 0.7, halo = TRUE)

Read the map

The index runs from 0.03 to 0.81 GP FTE per 1,000 residents. Averaged over residents it is 0.58, the same as the mainland’s 311 GP FTE for its 541,000 residents on the grid. As in the small example, the index shares out the supply and creates none.

It is highest in the bright band between Redruth, Truro and Falmouth, where several practices with many GP FTE lie within a short drive. It is lowest on Bodmin Moor, the dark patch north-east of Bodmin, and at the tips of the Land’s End peninsula, west of Penzance, and the Lizard, south of Helston. There the nearest practices are further away. Read the values along the border with Devon, at the right edge of the map, with care: the data cover Cornwall only, so the index leaves out the Devon practices that some residents there use, and the Devon residents who compete for Cornish practices.

The index compares GP supply with nearby demand and says nothing about who uses a practice, waiting times or the care received (Reading results explains).
